question: Which statement best describes loading.tsx (instant loading states)?
options: A `loading.tsx` in a route segment is automatically wrapped around that segment's `page.tsx` in a React `<Suspense>` boundary. While the async Server Component awaits data, Next streams the loading fallback to the browser instantly, then swaps in the real content when it's ready — no manual Suspense wiring needed.

An `error.tsx` is a Client Component (it must start with `'use client'`) that Next.js turns into an Error Boundary around the segment. If rendering the segment throws, Next renders `error.tsx` instead of crashing the whole app. It receives an `error` prop and a `reset()` function.

The `reset()` function passed to `error.tsx` re-attempts to render the segment's contents without a full page reload. It's the recovery path: a transient failure (a flaky fetch) can be retried in place, keeping the surrounding layout and navigation intact.

Calling the `notFound()` helper from a Server Component throws a special error that Next catches and renders the nearest `not-found.tsx` with a 404 status. It's the idiomatic way to say 'this resource doesn't exist' — e.g. an unknown product slug.

question: Which statement best describes error.tsx (per-segment error boundary)?
options: Calling the `notFound()` helper from a Server Component throws a special error that Next catches and renders the nearest `not-found.tsx` with a 404 status. It's the idiomatic way to say 'this resource doesn't exist' — e.g. an unknown product slug.

A segment-level `error.tsx` cannot catch errors thrown in the root layout itself, because it lives inside that layout. `global-error.tsx` is the last-resort boundary that wraps the entire app — it must render its own `<html>` and `<body>` because the broken layout is replaced.
